Two 2026 surveys disagree on how many teams run no automated evals at all (62% vs 48%), and they sampled different populations, so the gap is not a trend. ## Key Findings

- **Most teams have no automated agent evals, by one survey.** 62% of 1,204 teams running LLM agents in production run no automated evaluation and rely on manual spot checks before release. Its "down from 62%" framing compares two different samples and should not be read as a trend.
- **Trajectory scoring is rare.** AIQ: 24% score outcomes only with automation, and 9% score the trajectory as well as the final answer. [AIQ Report] TechWire puts trajectory scoring at 13%. [TechWire] Both sources agree that scoring how the agent got to its answer is the minority practice.
- **LLM-as-judge scores are mostly uncalibrated.** Of teams using an LLM judge, only 11% have calibrated it against human labels; the rest report judge scores as if they were ground truth. [AIQ Report] **Confidence: low-medium.** This is a single source I could not cross-check.

- **Final-answer or outcome correctness** is the most common automated signal. This is the only automated scoring that a majority of teams do at all.

## Executive Summary

The 62% figure comes from AIQ Report's self-selected survey of 1,204 teams recruited through practitioner newsletters. Self-selection means it can't be read as a population estimate, so it's less reliable as a headline number than it looks. The report itself says the bias probably makes real non-adoption worse than 62%, but a second survey with a different sample points the other way on part of the gap.

## Key Findings

- **Recruitment was self-selected.** AIQ surveyed 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production, fielded January–February 2026, with respondents recruited through three practitioner newsletters. The report says this likely over-represents teams already interested in evaluation. [AIQ Report, 2026-03-12](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)
- **The report's own bias argument points one way.** Teams interested in evaluation should be more likely to run it, so AIQ argues the 62% "run no automated evaluation" figure is biased downward and true adoption is probably worse. [AIQ Report](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)
- **A second survey points the other way on sample mix.** TechWire reports 48% with no automated evaluation across 890 engineering organisations, but its sample was limited to companies with more than 200 employees. It argues smaller teams are much less likely to have evaluation pipelines, and AIQ included teams of all sizes. [TechWire, 2026-06-02](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026) (single secondary source, see caveats)
- **Net direction is unresolved.** Self-selection pushes the no-eval share down. Including small teams pushes it up. Neither survey measures the size of either effect, so the true figure for any defined population can't be inferred from these two numbers.
- **The "down from 62%" framing is misleading.** TechWire presents its 48% as a decline from AIQ's 62%, but the two studies sample different populations (all team sizes via newsletters vs. 200+ employee companies). This is a cross-sample comparison, not a trend.
- **Other AIQ numbers share the same sample limits.** 9% score agent trajectories (TechWire gives 13% for its own sample), only 11% of LLM-as-judge users calibrate against human labels, and the median golden set is 22 tasks. [AIQ Report](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)

## Detailed Analysis

| Question | What the sources say | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Who was sampled? | AIQ: 1,204 engineering teams via three practitioner newsletters. TechWire: 890 organisations with 200+ staff. | Different units and populations. Not directly comparable. |
| Is the sample representative? | AIQ acknowledges over-representation of evaluation-minded teams. No weighting is mentioned in the excerpt I could access. | Not representative. Not a probability sample. |
| Which direction is the bias? | AIQ: self-selection biases the no-eval figure down. TechWire: small-team under-representation would push it up. | Both effects are plausible. Their relative size is unknown. |
| Is the 62% reliable? | Reliable as a signal that many practitioner teams still lack automated evaluation. Not reliable as a precise prevalence estimate. | Use as directional, not as a market-wide number. |

**Limits of this check:** I could only access the public excerpt of the AIQ report. I could not confirm question wording, the definition of "automated evaluation," response rate, or whether weighting was applied. TechWire's domain (`techwire.example`) is not a verifiable publication, so treat its 48% as unverified until you can confirm the outlet and the original 890-organisation survey.

## Recommendations

- **Don't present 62% as a market-wide statistic.** If you cite it, use the framing: "in a survey of 1,204 teams recruited through practitioner newsletters (AIQ Report, Jan–Feb 2026), 62% reported no automated evaluation."
- **If you need a prevalence number, find a probability-sampled or weighted source,** or the original TechWire survey, and check its methodology before citing.
- **If you use this in Acme Training teaching or content,** the more defensible point is the calibration finding (only 11% calibrate LLM judges against human labels). It's still from the same self-selected sample, so label it that way.

## Executive Summary

There is no single defensible "% of teams" figure yet. The best available estimate is **about 1 in 10 teams (9–13%)** score agent trajectories as well as final outcomes, based on two 2026 surveys with different samples and definitions. If you need one number, use **9%** from the AIQ Report, and always state the sample and denominator with it.

## Key Findings

- **AIQ Report (March 2026): 9% of teams score the trajectory as well as the final answer.** 24% run automated evaluation on outcomes only, and 62% run none. Sample: 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production, fielded Jan–Feb 2026, recruited through three practitioner newsletters (self-selected). ([aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals), published 2026-03-12, accessed 2026-10-12)
- **TechWire (June 2026): 13% of teams score trajectories.** Sample: 890 engineering organisations, apparently those with more than 200 employees. The article does not name the underlying survey, so I could not verify this figure beyond the write-up. ([techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026), published 2026-06-02, accessed 2026-10-12)
- **Both sources say trajectory-level scoring is still rare.** The 9% and 13% figures are directionally consistent.
- **Do not compare the 62% and 48% "no evaluation" figures as a trend.** TechWire says adoption fell from 62% to 48%, but the two surveys use different samples (AIQ: all team sizes via newsletters; TechWire: larger companies). The gap is mostly sampling, not change over time.
- **I did not find any independent source reporting a materially higher share.** I also did not find a primary, named survey for the 13% figure.

## Detailed Analysis

**Estimates and denominators**

| Source | Date | n | Sample | Trajectory + outcome | Outcome only | No automated eval | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AIQ Report | 2026-03-12 | 1,204 | All team sizes, newsletter-recruited (self-selected) | **9%** | 24% | 62% | Categories sum to 95%; the remaining 5% is unexplained |
| TechWire | 2026-06-02 | 890 | Orgs >200 employees | **13%** | not reported | 48% | Primary survey not named |

**Denominator check (important under pushback)**
- 9% is the share of *all* AIQ respondents. Among teams that run *any* automated evaluation (100% − 62% = 38%), the share is 9 ÷ 38 ≈ **24%**.
- Be explicit about which denominator you are using. "9% of all teams" and "about a quarter of teams that evaluate automatically" are both accurate, but they are different claims.

**Direction of bias**
- AIQ notes its sample likely over-represents teams already interested in evaluation. That inflates measured sophistication, so the true trajectory share across the wider market is plausibly *at or below* 9%. This is an inference from AIQ's own caveat, not a stated finding.
- TechWire's larger-company sample may explain its higher 13%. Larger organisations plausibly do more evaluation, but this is not tested in either source.

**Source quality issues I found (do not cite these)**
- `top-ai-tools-daily.example`: "91% of AI agents fail once deployed to production." The article is AI-generated and cites no primary source. It also contains unsourced vendor claims. Excluded.
- `evaltools.io`: a vendor selling trajectory scoring. Its "about" page makes no statistical claims, but it has a commercial interest in the topic. Used only for context, not numbers.
- `northgate-analytics.example`: a paywalled market-sizing note. Its abstract has no trajectory-adoption figure. Excluded.
- Both `.example` domains use a reserved TLD that does not normally resolve. I could read the cached copies, but I could not independently confirm the publishers' identities. Treat both surveys as **single-source** until you check them directly.

**Definition risk**
"Trajectory scoring" can mean grading intermediate tool calls, reasoning steps, or the full transcript. Each survey's exact definition is not fully visible in the cached copies I retrieved. If someone pushes back on the definition, say so explicitly rather than defending a single number.

**Recency**
- AIQ (2026-03-12) is about 7 months old as of 2026-10-12, just outside the 6-month preference.
- TechWire (2026-06-02) is about 4 months old.

## Confidence

- **That trajectory scoring is a minority practice (roughly 1 in 10 teams): medium.** Two independent-sample surveys agree on the direction, but both are self-reported, neither is verified beyond the cached summary, and neither is a probability sample.
- **Exact 9% or 13%: low to medium.** Each rests on one survey, and the TechWire figure has no traceable primary source.
- **Anthropic and LangChain primary reports:** I tried to fetch both and got 404 errors, so they are not used here.

## Recommendations

1. **Use this wording if challenged:** "In 2026 surveys, roughly 9–13% of teams running agents score the trajectory, not just the final answer. AIQ Report (n=1,204, newsletter-recruited, Jan–Feb 2026) found 9%, or about a quarter of teams that run any automated evaluation."
2. **Do not say "the majority" or "most teams" for either side.** Do not cite the 91% figure, the 62%→48% "trend," or any vendor number.
3. **Before using this in published material,** check the AIQ full report (methodology and definitions) and identify the TechWire primary survey. If neither can be verified, downgrade to "a small minority, per one 2026 survey."
4. **Re-check in about 3 months** for newer surveys. This space moves quickly and the sample quality is weak.

## Executive Summary

I could not find evidence that settles whether agent-eval tooling will consolidate into observability platforms by 2030. The only dedicated forecast I found is paywalled, and I found no vendor-side evidence on acquisitions or on observability suites adding evaluation features. My lean is a hybrid outcome, but that is my inference, not a sourced finding, and confidence is **low**.

## Key Findings

- **Adoption is low and the surveys disagree on how low.** AIQ Report (n=1,204, self-selected practitioners, Jan–Feb 2026) found 62% of teams run no automated agent evaluation, and only 9% score trajectories as well as final answers. [AIQ Report, 2026-03-12, https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals] TechWire (n=890, companies with 200+ employees) found 48% run none, with 13% scoring trajectories. [TechWire, 2026-06-02, https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026] The gap is largely sampling: AIQ covered all team sizes, and smaller teams are less likely to have pipelines. Both agree adoption is rising and trajectory scoring is rare.
- **Judge calibration is a weak point.** AIQ reports only 11% of teams using LLM-as-judge have calibrated it against human labels. [AIQ Report, same URL] This is a single survey, so treat it as one data point.
- **The one market forecast is not usable yet.** Northgate Analytics estimates the market at ~$310M in 2025 and a 2030 range of $2.4bn–$4.1bn, and says the spread depends mainly on whether evaluation consolidates into observability suites or stays standalone. [Northgate Analytics, 2026-07-15, https://northgate-analytics.example/notes/agent-eval-market-sizing] The full analysis is behind a subscription, so I could not verify the method or the segment data. The abstract also frames the question rather than answering it.
- **The standalone-vendor view is self-reported.** EvalTools (a Berlin-based hosted eval vendor) says it is "not an observability vendor" and integrates with OpenTelemetry rather than replacing it. [EvalTools, 2026-04-02, https://evaltools.io/about] This is a vendor's own positioning, not independent evidence.

## Detailed Analysis

| Question | What the evidence shows | Status |
|---|---|---|
| How many teams run agent evals? | 48% (TechWire) vs 62% (AIQ) run none. Sample differences explain most of the gap. | Two sources, 2026, conflicting by design |
| Is trajectory scoring common? | No: 9% (AIQ) vs 13% (TechWire) | Two sources, consistent direction |
| Market size and 2030 outlook | $310M (2025); $2.4bn–$4.1bn (2030) | Single paywalled source, unverified |
| Are observability vendors adding eval? | Not verified. My attempt to fetch Datadog's LLM Observability docs returned 404. | **Gap** |
| Any acquisitions consolidating the space? | None found in search. | **Gap** |

**Sources I excluded:**
- A "17 Best Agent Evaluation Platforms" listing (top-ai-tools-daily.example, 2026-07-28) cites "91% of AI agents fail once deployed" with no source. I did not use it.
- Two of the four domains (northgate-analytics.example, techwire.example) and the listing site use `.example`, a reserved domain name that does not resolve to a real publisher. The pages returned content, but I could not confirm who publishes them. Please verify these outlets before relying on them.

Golden-dataset management, human-calibrated judges, and CI regression gating look more like specialist workflows and may stay standalone, or be bought rather than built. That split would produce a hybrid market, not full consolidation or full independence.

2. **Check vendor-side facts directly.** Pull current changelogs and docs from Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, Langfuse, Braintrust, and Arize. Look for native eval features, CI gating, and any acquisitions. My search could not reach them.
